chunks: I wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), or said to him: 'May God make me your ransom! We worship the Beneficent, the Merciful, the One, the Singular, the Eternal.'

He [the narrator] said: So he [the Imam] said: 'Indeed, whoever worships the Name apart from the One Named by the Names has committed shirk, blasphemed, and denied — and has not worshipped anything at all. Rather, worship God, the One, the Singular, the Eternal, the Named One by these Names — not the Names [themselves]. The Names are attributes by which He described Himself.'

key_terms.أَشْرَكَ: Committed shirk — associating partners with God, the gravest theological error
key_terms.الصَّمَد: Al-Samad — the Eternal Self-Sufficient, one who needs no one while all need Him (Quran 112:2)
key_terms.الِاسْم: Name — the linguistic descriptor, distinct from the Named (al-musamma)
key_terms.الْمُسَمَّى: The Named One — God Himself, the actual Being designated by the Names
key_terms.صِفَات: Attributes — the Names are qualities God ascribes to Himself, not separate entities

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir say about worshipping God's names versus God Himself?
ai.summary: The narrator 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran poses a doctrinal question to Imam al-Baqir (AS): is it proper to direct worship toward the divine names themselves (al-Rahman, al-Rahim, al-Wahid, etc.)? The Imam's response clarifies a foundational principle of Shia theology: the Names of God are attributes (sifat) — descriptors that God uses of Himself — not independent beings or objects of worship. Directing devotion to the Names rather than to the One Being they describe constitutes shirk (associationism). This reflects the Shia theological position that God's essence is utterly distinct from, and irreducible to, His attributes or names.
